rules.text: One task name covers one real job that can be done in many correct ways. The description fixes what must be true, never how the operator does it.
These rules are for tasks created inside Verlet. A customer's tasks follow that customer's own rule set, kept as a separate group.
Task ID: a 3-letter code, a dash and a 3-digit number, then " · " and the task name. Example: LIQ-001 · Transfer red water into a 50 mL tube and close it.
Reverse ID: the same ID with R after the number. Example: LIQ-001R · Reset: Transfer red water into a 50 mL tube and close it.
Bunch (platform category): the group name, a 2-digit number and the family name, for example "Liquids 01 · Fill and close tubes". The reset bunch adds R: "Liquids 01R · Fill and close tubes".

Codes: LIQ liquids, LAB tubes racks and boxes, LID lids latches and cases, TOL tools and fasteners, CAB cables and wire, SRT look-alike sorting, HOM home desk and books, CLO clothing and hangers, PAK packing and wrapping, FIX replace and exchange. A new code is added only when no code fits.
One sentence in plain verbs that names the main items and the finished result. It never describes a method.

The Initial State lists each item, how it starts and its allowed start zones. All six zones are available by default. Restrict a particular start or work zone only for a real fit, reach, camera or fixed-equipment constraint, with a short reason for that item and zone in Zone limits. Separate a confirmed rig-test restriction from an untested concern. The team confirms or excludes states and zones after rig testing; never invent a reach restriction.

A start pose is written only when it creates work. A start variant may set a pose for that reason (a cup upside down that must be set upright, a box lying on its side that must stand); the Target State then names the end pose, and it holds for every variant. Otherwise the operator chooses how items lie. A start state the job depends on (cap on, lid closed, an item stacked on top) is written in "How it starts". Every item that opens or closes (bottle, box, case, jar, tube, lid, file, stapler, bag, tin) always has its state written: open or closed, cap on or off.

Every item has one role, and the role decides how it ends (rule 61). 10a The roles are: Product, Base, Source, Hand tool, Used tool, Tool with a home, Part, Part taken off, Leftover, Waste holder, Not used. 10b A task may list 1 or 2 Not used items on purpose: a look-alike, or a neighbour from the same job. Write them "not used, not touched". 10c The scene may also hold extra everyday items so it looks real and not staged (a mug, a book, a phone, tools from other jobs). Scene items are not listed one by one. None is a copy of a task item unless the task lists it as a look-alike. 10d No unused item, listed or scene, is ever used for the job. 10e An unused item may be set aside once, and only when it is really in the way: it touches or sits on a task item, it stands where the Product has to go, or it blocks the only way to reach a task item. It ends intact and in view. 10f Nothing, listed or scene, blocks the camera or the work. No liquid sits next to the RIVER power strip.

At most 5 steps. Each step is one goal: the item, what becomes true, and the visible end, for example "until the cap stops turning". A step names where an item goes only when the job needs it (into the rack, onto the bolt), never a zone by habit.
Parts of a step are joined with commas or "and", never "then".
Steps never say how to grab, which gripper to use, or at what angle to work.
Each item's full name is used once in a step. After that, "it" is allowed when it can only mean one item.

No step repeats what another step already says, and no instruction is given twice. Item names and required conditions are repeated wherever they are needed, so the steps, the Target State and the QC checks say the same thing in the same words.

The Target State is a table with three columns: Item, How it ends, End zone. Every item from the Initial State has a row. "How it ends" gives the condition the job created, the way a real worker leaves it when the job is done (closed, filled, stapled, back in its holder, set apart from the product). A pose is written only when it is the result of the job (folded, standing in the cup, set upright after starting upside down).
When more than one ending is correct, every correct ending is listed in "How it ends", joined with "or".
Everything the operator may choose freely is written in a Free line (for example "any order", "spines facing any side", "which corner"), so QC knows not to judge it.

QC checks every video in three looks. Each look tests conditions, never how the operator worked. The description carries the three looks as three blocks, in this order. 19a START CHECK, first frame, before the operator moves anything: every Initial State item is on the mat and in view; each is in its start condition or in one of the listed start variants; no part of the job is already done, meaning the Target State is not already true. Extra scene items are allowed (rule 10c). 19b DURING CHECK, while the video runs: no mistake from the standard list, and none of the task's own mistakes (rule 22). 19c END CHECK, last frame, once the operator has released the last item: every Target State row is true, including the quality line; every item rests still on the mat, none held, none at risk of falling; an item set aside rests still on the mat, intact and in view.

QC never fails a video for the method, the grip, the angle, a pose the task does not write, which zones were used, where the job ended, the order of steps that are not marked "before" or "after", fewer than three failed tries at an action, anything in the Free line, or the time alone. An episode over the reference time (rule 65) is a reason to look, never a reason to fail on its own: a longer episode done well, with real variation, passes.
Pass describes only what the last frame shows: every Target State row is seen. Falls and spills are judged during the video (rule 19b), not from the last frame.

Mistakes are one standard list plus 1 to 3 lines for the task. 22a Standard list: an item is dropped, anywhere; an item falls or is knocked over; liquid spills; something is forced, torn, bent or crushed, unless the job itself requires it and the Notes say so; the wrong item is used; an item the job does not use (listed or part of the scene) is used for the job, moved when it was not in the way, or moved more than once; an order the job forces ("before", "after") is broken; the operator stops and restarts; the third failed try at the same action; the same action is repeated with nothing changing, or there is movement that does no work on the job. 22b Task lines name concrete wrong results QC can see, for example "red water on the outside of the tube". 22c Fail lists at least three concrete wrong end results, separated by semicolons. 22d QC records each mistake by its name and the second it happened, so the team can see which mistakes happen most in each task. The platform's own idle measure flags an episode for review; a reviewer decides.

Operators are free to choose any allowed zone for each item's start and for the work, run by run. The Zone rotation in the Variation Sheet is a suggested plan, not an order. A run is 5 to 10 episodes with the same zones and the same start variant, changing how items are held, turned and placed every episode; the next run changes the zones of at least two items, the work zone, or the start variant.

By the end of each 2-hour block, every allowed zone has been used at least once as a start zone for each Product, and at least once as the work zone, and every start variant has been used at least once. The shift lead checks this from the run log; QC does not judge it per video. How the operator gets there is free.

A job ends where the job really ends. No item moves to a different zone only to satisfy a rule, and no step exists only to relocate a finished item. Every role ends as rule 61 says. Inside a container an item may face any direction and sit at any angle the container allows. Variety of position comes from varied starts and work zones, tracked under rules 23 and 24.
Zone lists include only zones the arms reach comfortably for that item, judged from its size and weight and the two-jaw 95 mm gripper.

Plain, simple English with short sentences. One name per item, taken from the Asset Pool when the item is there. Office tools keep the name printed on them (JAYO, INGCO, WISEUP, RIVER, Bosch, Ryobi, ANENG, TP-Link, Labshark).
No colours unless two items would otherwise be confused. Use each item as it is. Liquids are "red water".
No position words (middle, top, bottom, left, right, beside, side by side, in a row) unless the job needs them.
Every "until" ends at something visible: until it stops, until the edges meet, until it is empty, until it is fully inside, a count.

Banned words are the vague ones and the grip ones, never the words that name a real action. Banned: firmly, neatly, properly, correctly, carefully, gently, slowly, roughly, all the way, around (except "full turns around"), about, some, small, enough, as needed, if, lower, slide, let go, pinch, fingers, thumb, hand, tilt. Arms are never named.
Red water is standard; blue water is allowed for an episode and is never a separate task. Liquids never share a task with the power strip. Plastic before glass.
Only the big black nuts and bolts. Items inside boxes, bags or jars need light so they show on camera; bags are clear or white, never black. Drills are allowed but used simply. Fans are not used.

A tube is filled only while it stands in its rack or box. A tube taken out of a rack or box returns to the same hole or the same numbered well. Rack holes change each episode, so steps say "an empty hole". Cryobox wells are named by their printed corner numbers (81-hole box: 1, 9, 73, 81; 25-hole box: 1, 5, 21, 25), well 1 top-left in the camera view.

Each family has a clear Variation Sheet posted on every rig and read before the block. Its contents are listed in rule 65. Use additional pages when needed to retain all distinct realistic variants; readability must not remove valid possibilities.
Every rule has a number, a version and a date. A new or changed rule is checked against every other rule before it is saved; any clash is resolved first.
When a rule changes, every description written under an older version is flagged for review.

Every task uses the tool people really use for that job. Notes name the real tool, say whether it is in stock and whether it is easy to buy. If the real tool is hard to get, an improvised tool may be used, marked Improvised with the reason.
QC checks that the job was really done, the way a real worker would leave it, and that no listed mistake happened. How the operator did it never matters.
The order of steps is free, except where the job itself forces it (paper is gathered before it is stapled; a tube is filled before it is closed). Those steps say "before" or "after".
A task that uses up material (paper, staples, tape, tissue, water) says in its Notes what is used up and how much per episode. Material not in stock is listed under Needs.

The reset starts from the end of the forward episode and ends in a valid start: any listed start variant. If the job cannot be undone with real tools (something cut, torn, used up), or the forward task already ends in a valid start, no reset is written and the Notes say why.
A job already on the Verlet platform is not written again as a forward task; it may appear only as a reverse.

The bench has no tape lines. Operators and QC know the six zones by name. A zone is always written with its number: Supply (1), Tool (2), Used Equipment (3), Staging (4), Operation (5), Finished Goods (6).
Write the steps first. The instruction, Initial State, Target State, QC check, Pass and Fail are traced from the steps. If any two of them disagree, the task is fixed before it is saved.
A step or QC line never claims a result that no step made. A result in the middle of the job may be a QC line, for example the tube holds red water before it is closed.
Every part taken off during the job (cap, lid, wrapper, packaging) appears in the Target State with where it ends, unless a step puts it back.

QC lines and Pass name only what can be seen on the video at that moment, never hidden contents or past events. A count or a condition that the job later hides is checked at the moment it is visible (rule 19b) and is not claimed again in the END CHECK.

Liquid endpoints, in this order of choice: a natural end (the pipette is empty, the source is empty, full to the shoulder); the container's own printed scale; a tape ring on the container only when it has no scale and a partial level is the point of the task (3 to 5 mm wide, ends meeting, lower edge at the level).
Liquid amounts add up: the source amount, the number of fills and the space in the receiver agree, for the forward task and its reset. Overflow is tested before recording.
Every size, fit or reach fact that is not confirmed is listed under "Rig test first" and tested before recording. Sizes are never invented.

Start conditions are plain and easy to check. A tidy-up start is allowed (items scattered, open, outside their container), but never a half state (partly stuck, half open, raised corner, half pushed in). No task starts with a deliberate mistake; repair and swap jobs are written as replace or exchange jobs.
Counts are stated when QC can see them counted: in the last frame, or at the moment in the video when they are visible (rule 48). Up to 10 items, or groups of 5 up to 20. Dominoes come in 10 or 20.

In a look-alike task, the item that fits ends where the job puts it (in the holder, on the bolt); the item that does not fit ends not touched, or set apart from the product when it was tried and refused.

Use the everyday word for the job ("button a shirt", "staple the sheets", "pack the case"). The hard case is "closed shut". Steps use plain action verbs: the Controlled Vocabulary (grab, move, take out, put into, put in, put onto, turn, press, place, fill, squeeze, pour, open, close, wrap, fold, peel, tear, plug in, unplug, button, unbutton, zip, unzip, stack, hang, coil, lift, carry, push, pull, wipe, sweep) plus the everyday verb for the job when no listed verb names it, such as gather, staple, sort, hang, fasten, join or line up.
One task per kind of job; never two tasks that differ only in colour. Every task is a job clients worldwide would buy data for: real, manipulation-rich, simple to do, never senseless.
Items used in platform tasks count as in stock even when they are not in the Asset Pool.

Every Variation Sheet ends with the standard line: "If something goes wrong: if anything is dropped, knocked over, broken or spilled, stop, set up a valid start again and record again. A video with a mistake that is saved anyway is marked Failed, with the second it happened." Tasks do not repeat it.
Descriptions never contain reject codes, QC upload fields, camera instructions, the owner's name or a bunch number.
A task is Ready only when every check passes. After every 10 tasks the text is re-read from start to end.

End conditions follow the role, and the zone stays free. Product: Finished, where the job leaves it, or inside or onto what it goes into. Base: Changed by the job, not moved. Source: Closed again if it closes, holding less, where it started unless the job moves it. Hand tool (clean after use): Ready for the next person (closed, blade shut, tape retracted, switched off), resting on the mat, not touching the product; any zone. Used tool (dirty, wet or spent): Set apart from the product and clean items; any zone, or inside the waste holder when it is thrown out. Tool with a home: Back inside its home, the home closed if it closes. Part: In place on or in the product. Part taken off: Back on its item when the real job ends closed; otherwise a Leftover. Leftover: Inside the waste holder. Waste holder: Holding the waste, any zone. Not used: Where it started, not touched; or, when it was really in the way, set aside once and left intact and in view (rule 10e).

An item put into another item ends "inside the <item>". An item that stays ends "where it started". A zone is written in the Target State only for a Product, a Hand tool or a Used tool; every other role is judged by its condition, not its zone.
Only possible zones are listed, for start and end: zones the arms reach comfortably for that item, where it fits, and where the camera shows the result.

Every reset is its own task row with its own ID (LIQ-001R): its own instruction, Initial State (the forward Target State, word for word), Steps, Target State, Free line, QC check, Pass, Fail and Variation Sheet.

The Variation Sheet carries, for the family or for a single task when it needs its own: 65a 3 to 6 meaningful realistic task start states (rule 70), or a simple physical reason when fewer are possible. 65b All distinct realistic ways to do the job, and all distinct realistic ending arrangements, including uncommon but plausible ones. There is no fixed method or ending count, no numerical cap and no completion shortcut. Ending arrangements describe valid forms and relationships, and all satisfy the same Target State. 65c Real-world scenarios where people do this job, the QC freedoms, and the common mistakes. 65d A realistic reference time, researched from the job itself and from its variation, marked as an estimate until the rig test times it. It is a reference for how long the job takes when done well, never a limit. It is written in the Variation Sheet and in the task description. Time alone never fails an episode (rule 20). 65e The Zone map (rule 68), the Zone rotation (rule 69) and the specific reason for any excluded item, zone or state. 65f Every method listed is physically realistic for two-jaw 95 mm grippers; untested feasibility is stated honestly. Suggested methods and endings never restrict otherwise valid operator choices. Keep the sheet expandable as rig testing reveals more.
A task is finished only when every check passes. Failing checks are fixed and checked again; a task that still fails is marked Needs review and is not exported.

Every task names its work zone: the zone where the job itself is done (where the item is opened, filled, fastened or folded). It is open by default, "Any zone (1–6)"; Operation (5) is one choice, not the rule. When the job happens on an item that stays (a rack, a machine), the work zone is wherever that item stands. Steps never fix a zone for an item; when the zone matters they say "in the work zone".

The Variation Sheet carries a Zone map for every item and the work zone across zones 1 to 6. Record allowed starts and work zones according to item roles; endings follow the job (rule 25). Record each excluded combination with a short specific reason in Zone limits, and label it confirmed by rig test or still to test. Keep task start states separate from zone choices. The team updates restrictions after testing. Every allowed zone remains available and is covered in the run log under rule 24.

The Variation Sheet carries a Zone rotation: a suggested plan of up to 6 runs that together use every allowed zone as a start for each Product and as the work zone. Operators may follow it in any order or choose other allowed zones, as long as rule 24 is met. The app draws it.

Start variants: list 3 to 6 meaningful realistic task start states that change what the operator must do, such as open or closed, cap on or off, upside down, stacked, a different supported count, look-alikes or an obstructing scene item. These are task states, not zone numbers. If fewer realistic states are physically possible, state the simple reason rather than inventing variants. Every opening or closure has its start state written; include its other real state when appropriate. Each run records its selected state and zones. Every listed state is a valid QC start and leads to the same Target State. No half-finished setups or deliberate mistakes. The team may exclude a state after rig testing and records the specific reason.

A task that makes waste names its waste holder, chosen by what is real for that job: the tool's own catcher (a pencil sharpener's box, a hole punch's chip tray), the packaging the item came from, a tissue or paper plate, or a small bin or tray when nothing else is real. The waste holder is an item in the Initial State with the role Waste holder and stands in any zone. Waste never ends loose on the mat. A task that makes no waste writes "Waste holder: none".

QC judges every video against its task description and nothing else: a valid start, no listed mistake, every Target State row true at the end. QC records the result and its quality score on the platform, with the mistake and the second it happened. A video with a mistake is not delivered; it is kept with its notes for the mistake counts in rule 22d.

The last step states the final action and the visible finished condition it leaves. Use the same item names, condition words and placement as the corresponding Target State rows; every permitted ending must agree in both places. After the last step, every Target State row must be true, including required closures, tool states, removed parts and product placement; earlier steps must establish the conditions not created by the last action. Do not end with a vague instruction such as "finish the task", add a result no step creates, or narrow the allowed endings by inventing a pose, fixed zone or extra action. Keep the last step one clear goal within the five-step limit; do not copy the whole Target State table into it. Apply this to forward tasks and resets.

Brainstorm real jobs across different meaningful motions, not only different objects. Use this T-Rex reference checklist: grasp and lift; reach; lift and place; wrap; fold; press; insert; peel; wipe; squeeze; extract; disassemble; shake; dispense; pour; assemble; open; close; cut; screw; twist; unscrew. This is a starting taxonomy, not every possible motion. Add other clearly defined motions when real work requires them, such as stirring or threading. For each proposed job, name the primary motion that creates its result and the secondary motions that materially contribute. Routine reaching or transporting does not make two otherwise identical jobs different.

Compare proposed jobs with existing, selected and previously rejected jobs using object family × primary motion, secondary motions, contact or material behaviour, and finished result. State the useful coverage each candidate adds and the real-world reason for the job. Prefer underrepresented feasible combinations while keeping valuable jobs that combine skills. A colour, zone, object substitution or renamed motion is not automatically a new task. Keep ordinary and uncommon realistic variants without invented frequencies or a fixed count cap. Do not add pointless motions, require every motion in each task, or revive an owner-rejected task merely to fill a coverage gap. Motion coverage is a brainstorming and review aid, not a quota or a new per-video QC failure.

For each motion–object candidate, check the actual two-jaw 95 mm grippers, object dimensions, access, support, closures, tool availability, force or compliance needs, and observable completion. Mark feasibility as untested until demonstrated on the rig; record the specific reason for exclusions. T-Rex uses dexterous multi-finger hands and tactile sensing; its demonstrations do not establish feasibility or sensing capability on our rigs. Do not prescribe independent-finger actions or claim measured contact force, slip sensing or hidden outcomes without the corresponding evidence. Never introduce a deliberate drop, spill, damage or other prohibited mistake to obtain a motion example.

Keep motion labels, coverage comparisons and source references in brainstorming or review information. Operator steps remain short, outcome-based and method-free under the writing rules; research labels do not override banned wording, free zones, valid alternatives or the final-step/Target State rule. Use reference pages, taxonomy figures and demonstrable clips honestly: label what was read or viewed and what remains unverified. The T-Rex visualizer shows a random subset with trimmed, sometimes sped-up clips; its clip duration and displayed counts are not our task timing, rarity or production quota. Recheck sources when extending the reference and retain useful human real-work examples when a verified gripper demonstration is unavailable.

Every task conversation reads the current rules before writing or changing anything. When a rule does not fit the real job, or a customer's need calls for something else, ask before following it and say why: a rule that does not fit is changed, not worked around. The rules live in three places that must always carry the same version: the GitHub repo, the Claude artifact and the Codex app.
